page: Amazon Web Services r8g.medium is an entry-level memory-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro System and powered by the custom AWS Graviton4 Neoverse-V2 processor. Running on the arm64 architecture, this virtual machine provisions 1 dedicated physical core and 1 vCPU operating at 2.8 GHz, complemented by 64 KB L1d cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and a 36 MB L3 cache pool. It provides 8.0 GB of RAM, maintaining an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio characteristic of AWS memory-optimized tiers. Networking is provisioned with a 1 Gbps baseline bandwidth. The instance features no integrated local storage and contains no discrete GPU hardware.

Benchmark evaluations indicate consistent single-threaded compute output matching its single dedicated core allocation. In single-core tests, the Graviton4 core registers average results with a stress-ng score of 1687.88 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1745.0. It also shows competitive throughput in bzip3 decompression at 14.2 GB/sec and gzip compression at 30.43 GB/sec. However, because the instance operates with only 1 vCPU, aggregate throughput benchmarks such as multi-core stress-ng (1687.88), PassMark overall CPU (987.01), and compilation with Clang (2220.0) fall into lower comparative percentiles relative to multi-core instances.

Memory bandwidth measurements achieve 115.67 GB/sec for small cached blocks, tapering to 30.2 GB/sec for uncached reads and 11.94 GB/sec for large writes. In operational tests, the single-core configuration achieves 2.14 million operations per second in Redis SET workloads and 2.4 GB/sec in static web serving, alongside a PassMark database operations metric of 1485.8. For small language models (135M parameters), it delivers 76.05 prompt processing tokens per second and 56.99 generation tokens per second.

From an infrastructure perspective, r8g.medium provides a cost-efficient entry point into modern arm64 Graviton4 architectures when memory density takes precedence over raw parallel processing. Its lack of included local ephemeral storage means workloads depend entirely on external networked block devices. The hardware profile suits lightweight in-memory databases, small Redis caching nodes, staging environments, message brokers, and auxiliary services that need 8 GB of memory without requiring multiple compute cores.
